author: ValWood
body:
For example

transcription coactivator activity

seems weak from the abstract:

Isolation and characterization of ARA160 as the first androgen receptor N- terminal-associated coactivator in human prostate cells.

Abstract
The androgen receptor (AR) is a member of the steroid receptor superfamily that may require coactivators for proper or maximal transactivation. Using a purified AR N-terminal peptide as a probe to screen the human testis expression library, we identified an androgen-enhanced AR N-terminal-associated protein ARA160, which consists of 1,093 amino acids with an apparent molecular mass of 160 kDa. Sequence comparison in GenBank(TM) reveals that ARA160 shares an identical sequence with a HIV-1 TATA element modulatory factor, TMF. The far-Western blotting and co-immunoprecipitation assays demonstrate that the AR can interact directly with ARA160/TMF. Affinity gel pull-down and mammalian two-hybrid assays further suggest androgen can enhance significantly the interaction between AR and ARA160. Transient transfection assays demonstrated that **ARA160 might function as a coactivator for AR-mediated transactivation** in human prostate cancer PC-3 cells. Our data further suggest that this AR N-terminal coactivator can function cooperatively with AR C-terminal coactivator, ARA70, in PC-3 cells. Together, our data demonstrate that ARA160 **might represent the first identified androgen-enhanced N-terminal coactivator for the AR**.

author: colinlog
body:
Drew et al 2018 (PMID: 28596423) who integrated >9000 mass spectrometry datasets to computationally generate protein complexes (version huMAP1.0) had TMF1 in two complexes with two dbTFs (CEBPA and FOXP1). This has been replaced by huMAP2.0

In huMAP 2.0 there are 3 TMF1 complexes 

[HuMAP2_02900](https://humap2.proteincomplexes.org/displayComplexes?complex_key=HuMAP2_02900) 
[HuMAP2_03919](https://humap2.proteincomplexes.org/displayComplexes?complex_key=HuMAP2_03919) 
[HuMAP2_05932](https://humap2.proteincomplexes.org/displayComplexes?complex_key=HuMAP2_05932).

HuMAP2_05932 has CEBPA (again) but not FOXP1 and nor AR (but you need a steroid hormone for that one).
I would therefore not immediately dismiss the transcription annotation although, of course, when solely looking at protein complex compositions there cannot be direct functional evidence for 'co-activation' as would be implied by a GO:0003712 annotation. Interstingly, CEBPA does bind to multiple members of the 5932 complex (CCDC183, RABEP1, RUNDC1, TMF1, TEDC1). Notably, this is the only CEBPA-bearing complex in huMAP 2.0. So we are not likely to be looking at an instance of promiscuous-protein-binding by CEBPA.

As CCDC183 has no GO-CC and no known function, RABEP1 is found in early endosomes, RUNDC1 may work with dbTF p53 but has no GO-CC, and TEDC1 is at the base of the cilium / centrosomal I am not sure what to say about this automatically generated protein complex except to say that TMF annotation for transcription regulation is weakly if at all strengthened by this protein complex.

The 1999 JBC paper is very good, however, Val !!! They show that the co-activation they document for AR is also true for the gluccorticoid receptor and for the progesterone receptor on the same MMTV reporter. They conclusively show dbTF dependence, steroid dependence and repeat their result in multiple cell lines. Importantly, on Figure 4B even AR activation domain specificity is shown. Therefore, the JBC results demonstrate that it was not a 'golgi-mediated-general-boost-in-steroid receptor-assay-output', if you see what I mean.  It is specific to the AF1 transcription activation domain of AR and works without added steroid when dissociated form the ligand binding domain part of AR. 

There is something else, however. The authors state (data not shown) that a Gal4-DNA binding domain fusion to TMF1 does not work as a dbTF. This is not consistent with a transcription factor co-activator molecular function as defined in GO:0003712 and child terms. The authors 'hand wave' that it might be a co-activator that requires something else that the AF1 domain of steroid receptors can recruit. I believe that the AF1 domains works together with MAPK-type kinases, so it is not an entirely implausible reaso ning line, but untested here.

All in all, TMF1/ARA160 annotation to transcription can be deprioritized for now, but in my view it should certainly not be dismissed entirely. 

Last tidbit: the ARA70 co-activator for the estrogen receptor in that same 1999 study is also a cargo receptor and, in 2014 that was shown to affect nuclear replication quite convincingly. Essentially it appears to me that there may still be some unsolved molecular biology mysteries surrounding cargo receptors that moonlight as chromatin factors.

author: ValWood
body:
OK, agreed, this is the Claude summary:


The evidence that TMF1 acts as a transcription coregulator is real but modest and somewhat dated — it comes from a limited number of studies, relies heavily on overexpression and biochemical binding assays, and the protein's primary identity has since shifted toward vesicular trafficking. Here's a breakdown:

What the evidence actually shows
1. TBP inhibition (1992) — The protein was originally cloned as a factor that binds the HIV-1 TATA element and inhibits transcriptional activation by the TATA-binding protein (TBP). This is the origin of its name, but it was characterised in a viral context (HIV-1 LTR), not in regulation of endogenous genes.
2. Androgen receptor coactivation — The strongest transcriptional evidence comes from a 1999 study identifying TMF1 as ARA160, the first androgen receptor N-terminal-associated coactivator in human prostate cells. Far-Western blotting and co-immunoprecipitation assays demonstrated that the AR can interact directly with ARA160/TMF, and affinity gel pull-down and mammalian two-hybrid assays further suggest androgen can enhance the interaction. Transient transfection assays demonstrated that ARA160 might function as a coactivator for AR-mediated transactivation in human prostate cancer PC-3 cells. Note the hedged language throughout ("might function").
3. Association with the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex — A 2002 study showed that hbrm/hSNF2α and BRG-1/hSNF2β, the ATPase subunits of the human SNF/SWI complexes, specifically associate in vitro and in vivo with TMF/ARA160. This interaction requires highly conserved N-terminal regions of the SNF2 subunits and a C-terminal region of TMF/ARA160. This is mechanistically suggestive, though the physiological significance was not established.
4. PDGFRβ-dependent chromatin remodelling — A 2018 study (PMID 29545370) provided newer evidence that PDGFRβ translocates to the nucleus and regulates chromatin remodelling via TATA element-modifying factor 1, offering a more recent and independent angle.

Reasons to be cautious

Databases consistently use hedged language: potential coactivator of the androgen receptor, not confirmed coactivator.
The NIH Pharos target database classifies TMF1 as "Tbio" — a category for proteins about which virtually nothing is known in terms of drug or functional characterisation.
Most of the transcription evidence comes from transient transfection and overexpression assays, which are prone to artefacts and don't prove endogenous function.
The bulk of post-2007 research has focused on TMF1's well-established role in Golgi biology: various identities have been assigned to TMF such as a potential coactivator of the androgen receptor, an SNF component of the SNF/SWI transcription factor complex, a transient associate of the tyrosine kinase Fer that mediates Stat3 degradation — but most mechanistic work has centred on Rab6-dependent retrograde membrane traffic from endosomes to the Golgi apparatus and from the Golgi to the ER.
TMF1's predominant subcellular localisation is the Golgi, not the nucleus, which complicates its role as a conventional coregulator.

Bottom line
The evidence is suggestive but not definitive. There are reproducible protein–protein interactions with AR and SWI/SNF components, and reporter assays are consistent with a coactivator role. But most studies are two decades old, used overexpression systems, and the GO annotation "transcription coregulator activity" appears to trace back to these same early studies. No systematic genomic or transcriptomic analyses (e.g. ChIP-seq, knockout RNA-seq in relevant tissues) have been published to nail down its endogenous targets or mechanisms. It would be reasonable to treat the transcriptional coregulator function as a credible but unconfirmed secondary role of a protein whose primary biology lies in vesicular trafficking.

I would focus on the  mechanistically confirmed role, and mention the potential co regulator role.
